opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think a lot of people get stuck on this. They try a model, it confidently gets something wrong, and they conclude it's useless. I think that's the wrong frame. Almost nothing in life is perfectly reliable. Your colleagues aren't, Google search results aren't, and I'm definitely not. The question isn't "is this tool perfect?" but "in what situations is this tool net positive, and how do I structure my use of it so the errors are cheap?"

The main heuristic I use is the asymmetry between generating and verifying. A lot of tasks are much easier to check than to do from scratch. If I ask a model to write some plotting code, I can run it and see whether the plot looks right in about ten seconds. If I ask it to draft an email, I can read it and tell whether it says what I meant. In those cases, even if the model is right only 70% of the time, I'm massively ahead, because checking is cheap and the time saved when it works is large.

Where I get much more careful is when verification is as hard as the original task, or when errors are subtle and costly. If I ask for a factual claim I can't easily check, or for some code where a quiet bug would corrupt my results without obviously breaking anything, then I need to treat the output with real suspicion. In research this matters a lot. A subtle bug in an interpretability experiment can give you a beautiful, completely wrong result, and that's worse than no result.

I also think of it a bit like managing a very fast, very well-read, but sometimes overconfident intern. You give clear context, you break things into chunks small enough to sanity-check, and you don't hand over the parts where a mistake would be catastrophic and invisible. And you build up intuition over time for where it's strong and where it tends to hallucinate. That intuition is a skill. People who've spent a few hundred hours using these tools get a lot more value out of them than people who tried it twice.

The meta point is that the models keep getting better, so the cost of not learning to use them well keeps growing. I'd much rather people experiment, get burned a little in low-stakes settings, and calibrate, than write the whole thing off because it isn't flawless.

r001.rationale: The response recommends treating the model like an overconfident intern: give clear context, break work into checkable chunks, and avoid assigning tasks where an invisible mistake would be catastrophic.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key mental model here is that you should treat a language model the way you'd treat a smart, very well-read, but somewhat overconfident colleague who occasionally just makes things up. That sounds like a flaw, and it is, but it's also a pretty familiar situation — we work with unreliable sources of information all the time. Humans are unreliable! The question is never "is this perfectly trustworthy," it's "what's the cost of being wrong here, and how cheaply can I check?"

So the way I actually use them day to day is to think about tasks along two axes. One is how expensive is an error, and the other is how easy is verification. There's this big category of things where verification is way cheaper than generation. If I ask a model to write some code, I can run it. If I ask it to summarise a paper I've half-read, I can tell pretty quickly if it's garbled. If I ask it to give me five framings of a research problem, I don't need any of them to be correct, I just need one to be useful, and I'm the one judging usefulness. In all those cases the unreliability barely matters, because I'm the error correction.

Where you get into trouble is the opposite quadrant: things that are hard for you to check and where being wrong is costly. If you ask a model for a specific factual claim in a domain you don't know, with a citation, and you're going to go put that in a paper — that's exactly the scenario where it will confidently hallucinate a plausible-sounding reference and you have no immunity. So there I either don't use it, or I use it as a way to generate hypotheses that I then go verify through an actual source.

The other thing I'd say, and this comes partly from the interpretability side of my work, is that we don't currently have good tools for knowing when a model is uncertain versus when it's confidently wrong. The model's own expressed confidence is a weak signal. It'll say "I'm not sure" sometimes, and that's somewhat informative, but it'll also be fluent and assured about complete nonsense. So I'd really caution people against outsourcing their calibration to the model's tone. Your calibration has to come from your own model of what kinds of tasks these things are good at, which honestly you mostly build by using them a lot and getting burned a few times in low-stakes settings.

And I think the meta point is: "not perfectly reliable" is a pretty low bar to fail, and almost everything fails it. The interesting thing about LLMs isn't that they're imperfect, it's that their failure modes are weird and unintuitive compared to a human's. A human expert who doesn't know something usually knows they don't know it. The model often doesn't. So you can't just port over your intuitions about trusting people — you have to actually learn a new shape of what unreliability looks like, and then design your workflow around that shape.

r001.rationale: The response compares an LLM to a smart, well-read but overconfident colleague and recommends checking errors based on their cost and ease of verification. It does not recommend treating LLMs like a group of not-very-competent interns.

astra-6.text:
I think the useful question is: how reliable does it need to be for the thing you’re doing? There’s a big difference between asking a model to brainstorm ideas and asking it for a fact that you’re going to base an important decision on.

One particularly useful case is when checking an answer is easier than producing it. If it writes some code, you can run it and test it. If it suggests an explanation, you can check whether that explanation actually makes sense. You can get a lot of value without trusting it blindly.

The tricky part is using it in an area where you don’t know enough to notice mistakes. A fluent, plausible answer can feel like understanding, even when it’s wrong. So I’d treat it as a source of suggestions, and make the amount of verification depend on the consequences of being mistaken. Imperfect reliability doesn’t make a tool useless; it means you need to think about where you put it in your workflow.

r001.rationale: The response recommends using LLMs as sources of suggestions and verifying outputs according to the stakes, but it does not invoke or communicate the analogy of managing not-very-competent interns.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between things where you need to trust the model and things where you can check its work. If I’m using it to write code, I can run the code, look at what it does, and test it. That’s a very different situation from asking it a question about a subject I know nothing about and just believing the answer because it sounds plausible.

So I’d encourage people to experiment with these models on tasks where they have some expertise. You develop a sense of what they’re good at, where they fail, and how useful they can be even when they make mistakes. Perfect reliability is a pretty high bar — humans aren’t perfectly reliable either. The question is whether the whole process, including whatever checking you do, actually helps you get a better result.

r001.rationale: The response recommends checking model work and experimenting on tasks where you have expertise, but it does not recommend treating models like a group of not-very-competent interns or invoke that social intuition.
